name: Fermat's Little Theorem
original_full_statement: If p is a prime number and a is an integer not divisible by p, then a^(p-1) is congruent to 1 modulo p.
hypotheses: p is a prime number
a is an integer
a is not divisible by p
conclusion: a^(p-1) is congruent to 1 modulo p

name: Lagrange's Theorem
original_full_statement: If G is a finite group and H is a subgroup of G, then the order of H divides the order of G.
hypotheses: G is a finite group
H is a subgroup of G
conclusion: The order of H divides the order of G

name: First Isomorphism Theorem for Rings
original_full_statement: If R and S are rings and f: R -> S is a ring homomorphism, then the quotient ring R/ker(f) is isomorphic to the image of f.
hypotheses: R and S are rings
f is a ring homomorphism from R to S
conclusion: The quotient ring R/ker(f) is isomorphic to the image of f

name: Order of a Finite Field
original_full_statement: If F is a finite field, then the number of elements in F is p^n for some prime number p and positive integer n.
hypotheses: F is a field
F has a finite number of elements
conclusion: The number of elements in F is p^n for some prime number p and positive integer n

name: Wilson's Theorem
original_full_statement: If p is a prime number, then (p-1)! is congruent to -1 modulo p.
hypotheses: p is an integer strictly greater than 1
p is a prime number
conclusion: (p-1)! is congruent to -1 modulo p

name: Cauchy's Theorem
original_full_statement: If G is a finite group and p is a prime number that divides the order of G, then G contains an element of order p.
hypotheses: G is a finite group
p is a prime number
p divides the order of G
conclusion: G contains at least one element of order p

name: Finite Integral Domain Theorem
original_full_statement: Every finite integral domain is a field.
hypotheses: R is a finite ring
R is a commutative ring with identity 1 != 0
R has no zero divisors
conclusion: R is a field

name: Chinese Remainder Theorem
original_full_statement: If m and n are coprime positive integers, and a and b are any integers, then the system of congruences x = a (mod m) and x = b (mod n) has a unique solution modulo mn.
hypotheses: m and n are positive integers
m and n are coprime
a and b are integers
conclusion: The system of congruences x = a (mod m) and x = b (mod n) has a unique solution modulo mn

name: Maximal Ideal Quotient Theorem
original_full_statement: If R is a commutative ring with identity and M is a maximal ideal of R, then the quotient ring R/M is a field.
hypotheses: R is a commutative ring with identity
M is a maximal ideal of R
conclusion: The quotient ring R/M is a field

name: Orbit-Stabilizer Theorem
original_full_statement: If a finite group G acts on a finite set X, and x is an element of X, then the order of G is equal to the size of the orbit of x multiplied by the size of the stabilizer of x.
hypotheses: G is a finite group
X is a finite set
G acts on the set X
x is an element of X
conclusion: The order of G is equal to the size of the orbit of x multiplied by the size of the stabilizer of x

name: Euler's Theorem
original_full_statement: Let n be a positive integer and a be an integer coprime to n. Then a raised to the power of the Euler totient function of n is congruent to 1 modulo n.
hypotheses: n is a positive integer
a is an integer
the greatest common divisor of a and n is 1
conclusion: a^{\phi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod n

name: Index 2 Subgroup Theorem
original_full_statement: Let G be a group and H be a subgroup of G. If the index of H in G is 2, then H is a normal subgroup of G.
hypotheses: G is a group
H is a subgroup of G
the index [G:H] is exactly 2
conclusion: H is a normal subgroup of G

name: Euclidean Domain implies Principal Ideal Domain
original_full_statement: If R is a Euclidean domain, then R is a Principal Ideal Domain (PID).
hypotheses: R is an integral domain
R is equipped with a Euclidean function (R is a Euclidean domain)
conclusion: Every ideal in R is generated by a single element

name: Cyclic Multiplicative Group Theorem for Finite Fields
original_full_statement: The multiplicative group of non-zero elements of any finite field is a cyclic group.
hypotheses: F is a field
F contains finitely many elements
conclusion: The group of units F^\times is a cyclic group

name: Center of a p-group Theorem
original_full_statement: Let G be a finite group whose order is a power of a prime number p. If G is not the trivial group, then the center of G is non-trivial.
hypotheses: G is a group
the order of G is p^n for some prime number p and integer n \geq 1
conclusion: The center Z(G) contains an element other than the identity

name: Boolean Ring Commutativity Theorem
original_full_statement: Let R be a ring in which every element is idempotent. Then R is a commutative ring.
hypotheses: R is a ring
for every element x in R, x^2 = x
conclusion: For all x, y in R, xy = yx

name: Euclid's Lemma
original_full_statement: If a prime number p divides the product of two integers a and b, then p divides a or p divides b.
hypotheses: p is a prime number
a and b are integers
p divides the product ab
conclusion: p divides a or p divides b

name: Cyclic Group Commutativity Theorem
original_full_statement: If a group G is cyclic, then G is an abelian group.
hypotheses: G is a group
there exists an element g in G such that every element of G is a power of g
conclusion: G is abelian

name: Characteristic Zero Perfect Field Theorem
original_full_statement: Every field of characteristic 0 is a perfect field.
hypotheses: F is a field
the characteristic of F is 0
conclusion: Every algebraic extension of F is separable

name: Principal Ideal Domain implies Unique Factorization Domain
original_full_statement: Every principal ideal domain (PID) is a unique factorization domain (UFD).
hypotheses: R is an integral domain
every ideal in R is principal
conclusion: R is a unique factorization domain

name: Subgroup of a Cyclic Group Theorem
original_full_statement: Every subgroup of a cyclic group is itself a cyclic group.
hypotheses: G is a cyclic group
H is a subgroup of G
conclusion: H is a cyclic group

name: Abelian Quotient Theorem
original_full_statement: If the quotient group of a group by its center is cyclic, then the group is abelian.
hypotheses: G is a group
Z(G) is the center of G
The quotient group G/Z(G) is cyclic
conclusion: G is an abelian group

name: Normal Subgroup Commutativity Theorem
original_full_statement: If H and K are normal subgroups of a group G and their intersection is trivial, then every element of H commutes with every element of K.
hypotheses: G is a group
H is a normal subgroup of G
K is a normal subgroup of G
The intersection of H and K is the trivial subgroup containing only the identity element
conclusion: For all h in H and k in K, the equation hk = kh holds

name: Prime Ideal Quotient Theorem
original_full_statement: Let R be a commutative ring with identity and I be a proper ideal of R. The quotient ring R/I is an integral domain if and only if I is a prime ideal.
hypotheses: R is a commutative ring with identity
I is a proper ideal of R
conclusion: The quotient ring R/I is an integral domain if and only if I is a prime ideal

name: Integral Domain Characteristic Theorem
original_full_statement: The characteristic of an integral domain is either 0 or a prime number.
hypotheses: R is an integral domain
conclusion: The characteristic of R is either 0 or a prime number

name: Units of a Polynomial Ring Theorem
original_full_statement: If R is an integral domain, then the group of units of the polynomial ring R[x] is exactly the group of units of R.
hypotheses: R is an integral domain
R[x] is the polynomial ring in one variable over R
conclusion: An element is a unit in R[x] if and only if it is a constant polynomial that is a unit in R

name: Tower Law for Field Extensions
original_full_statement: If E is a finite extension of a field F, and K is a finite extension of E, then K is a finite extension of F and the degrees satisfy [K:F] = [K:E][E:F].
hypotheses: F is a field
E is a field extension of F such that the degree [E:F] is finite
K is a field extension of E such that the degree [K:E] is finite
conclusion: K is a finite field extension of F, and [K:F] = [K:E] * [E:F]

name: Primitive Element Theorem
original_full_statement: Every finite extension of a field of characteristic zero is a simple extension.
hypotheses: F is a field
The characteristic of F is 0
E is a finite field extension of F
conclusion: There exists an element a in E such that E = F(a)

name: Rational Root Theorem
original_full_statement: If a polynomial with integer coefficients has a rational root p/q in lowest terms, then p divides the constant term and q divides the leading coefficient.
hypotheses: P(x) is a polynomial of degree n >= 1 with integer coefficients
The constant term a_0 of P(x) is non-zero
The leading coefficient a_n of P(x) is non-zero
p/q is a rational root of P(x)
p and q are integers such that their greatest common divisor is 1
conclusion: p divides a_0 and q divides a_n

name: First Supplement to the Law of Quadratic Reciprocity
original_full_statement: For any odd prime p, -1 is a quadratic residue modulo p if and only if p is congruent to 1 modulo 4.
hypotheses: p is an odd prime number
conclusion: -1 is a quadratic residue modulo p if and only if p is congruent to 1 modulo 4

name: Alternating Group Simplicity Theorem
original_full_statement: The alternating group A_n is simple for all n >= 5.
hypotheses: G is the alternating group A_n
n is an integer
conclusion: G is a simple group.

name: Direct Product of Cyclic Groups Theorem
original_full_statement: Let G and H be finite cyclic groups. The direct product G x H is cyclic if and only if the orders of G and H are coprime.
hypotheses: G is a finite cyclic group
H is a finite cyclic group
The greatest common divisor of the order of G and the order of H is 1
conclusion: The direct product G x H is a cyclic group.

name: Fermat's Theorem on Sums of Two Squares
original_full_statement: An odd prime p can be expressed as the sum of two integer squares if and only if p is congruent to 1 modulo 4.
hypotheses: p is a prime number
p is an odd integer
p is congruent to 1 modulo 4
conclusion: There exist integers x and y such that p = x^2 + y^2.

name: Second Supplement to the Law of Quadratic Reciprocity
original_full_statement: For an odd prime p, 2 is a quadratic residue modulo p if and only if p is congruent to 1 or 7 modulo 8.
hypotheses: p is a prime number
p is an odd integer
p is congruent to either 1 or 7 modulo 8
conclusion: 2 is a quadratic residue modulo p.

name: Idempotents of an Integral Domain Theorem
original_full_statement: In an integral domain, the only idempotent elements are 0 and 1.
hypotheses: R is an integral domain
e is an element of R
e is an idempotent element, meaning e^2 = e
conclusion: e is equal to 0 or e is equal to 1.

name: Polynomial Ring over a UFD Theorem
original_full_statement: If R is a unique factorization domain, then the polynomial ring R[x] is also a unique factorization domain.
hypotheses: R is a commutative ring with identity
R is a unique factorization domain
conclusion: The polynomial ring R[x] is a unique factorization domain.

name: Linear Congruence Solutions Theorem
original_full_statement: The linear congruence ax ≡ b (mod n) has exactly d incongruent solutions modulo n if and only if d = gcd(a, n) divides b.
hypotheses: a, b, and n are integers
d is the greatest common divisor of a and n
d divides b
conclusion: The linear congruence ax ≡ b (mod n) has exactly d incongruent solutions modulo n.

name: Order of Coprime Commuting Elements Theorem
original_full_statement: Let G be a group and let a, b be elements of G. If a and b commute and have coprime orders, then the order of ab is the product of the orders of a and b.
hypotheses: G is a group
a and b are elements of G
a and b commute, meaning ab = ba
The orders of a and b are finite
The greatest common divisor of the order of a and the order of b is 1
conclusion: The order of the product ab is equal to the product of the order of a and the order of b.

name: Sylow's Third Theorem
original_full_statement: Let G be a finite group of order p^n m, where p is a prime and p does not divide m. The number of Sylow p-subgroups of G, denoted n_p, divides m and is congruent to 1 modulo p.
hypotheses: G is a finite group
The order of G is p^n * m
p is a prime number
p does not divide m
n_p is the number of Sylow p-subgroups of G
conclusion: n_p divides m and n_p is congruent to 1 modulo p.

name: Comaximal Ideals Intersection Theorem
original_full_statement: Let R be a commutative ring with identity. If I and J are comaximal ideals of R (meaning I + J = R), then their intersection I ∩ J is equal to their product IJ.
hypotheses: R is a commutative ring with identity
I and J are ideals of R
I and J are comaximal, meaning the sum of ideals I + J is equal to R
conclusion: The intersection of I and J is equal to the product ideal IJ.

name: Sylow's First Theorem
original_full_statement: Let G be a finite group of order p^n m, where p is a prime number and p does not divide m. Then G contains at least one subgroup of order p^n.
hypotheses: G is a finite group
The order of G is p^n * m, where p is a prime and n >= 1
p does not divide m
conclusion: G contains a subgroup of order p^n

name: Eisenstein's Criterion
original_full_statement: Let R be a unique factorization domain and let f(x) = a_n x^n + a_{n-1} x^{n-1} + ... + a_0 be a polynomial in R[x]. If there exists a prime element p in R such that p divides a_i for all 0 <= i < n, p does not divide a_n, and p^2 does not divide a_0, then f(x) is irreducible over the field of fractions of R.
hypotheses: R is a unique factorization domain
f(x) = a_n x^n + a_{n-1} x^{n-1} + ... + a_0 is a polynomial in R[x]
There exists a prime element p in R
p divides a_i for all 0 <= i < n
p does not divide a_n
p^2 does not divide a_0
conclusion: f(x) is irreducible over the field of fractions of R

name: Cayley's Theorem
original_full_statement: Every group G is isomorphic to a subgroup of the symmetric group acting on G.
hypotheses: G is a group
conclusion: G is isomorphic to a subgroup of the symmetric group Sym(G)

name: Bézout's Identity
original_full_statement: Let a and b be integers, not both zero. Then there exist integers x and y such that ax + by = gcd(a, b).
hypotheses: a and b are integers
a and b are not both zero
conclusion: There exist integers x and y such that ax + by is equal to the greatest common divisor of a and b

name: Euler's Criterion
original_full_statement: Let p be an odd prime and let a be an integer coprime to p. Then a is a quadratic residue modulo p if and only if a^{(p-1)/2} ≡ 1 (mod p).
hypotheses: p is an odd prime
a is an integer
a and p are coprime
conclusion: a is a quadratic residue modulo p if and only if a^{(p-1)/2} is congruent to 1 modulo p

name: Roots of Polynomials over an Integral Domain
original_full_statement: Let R be an integral domain and let f(x) be a non-zero polynomial in R[x] of degree n. Then f(x) has at most n distinct roots in R.
hypotheses: R is an integral domain
f(x) is a polynomial in R[x]
f(x) is a non-zero polynomial
The degree of f(x) is n
conclusion: f(x) has at most n distinct roots in R

name: Transitivity of Algebraic Extensions
original_full_statement: Let F, K, and L be fields such that F is a subfield of K and K is a subfield of L. If K is an algebraic extension of F and L is an algebraic extension of K, then L is an algebraic extension of F.
hypotheses: F, K, and L are fields
F is a subfield of K
K is a subfield of L
K is an algebraic extension of F
L is an algebraic extension of K
conclusion: L is an algebraic extension of F

name: Burnside's Lemma
original_full_statement: Let G be a finite group that acts on a finite set X. Then the number of orbits of the action is equal to 1/|G| sum_{g in G} |X^g|, where X^g is the set of elements in X fixed by g.
hypotheses: G is a finite group
X is a finite set
G acts on the set X
conclusion: The number of distinct orbits of the action of G on X is equal to the average number of points fixed by the elements of G

name: Wedderburn's Little Theorem
original_full_statement: Every finite division ring is a commutative field.
hypotheses: R is a finite ring
R is a division ring
conclusion: R is a commutative field

name: Degree of a Simple Extension Theorem
original_full_statement: Let E/F be a field extension and let alpha in E be an element algebraic over F. If p(x) in F[x] is the minimal polynomial of alpha over F, then the degree of the simple extension [F(alpha) : F] is equal to the degree of p(x).
hypotheses: F is a field
E is an extension field of F
alpha is an element of E
alpha is algebraic over F
p(x) is the minimal polynomial of alpha over F
conclusion: The degree of the field extension [F(alpha) : F] is equal to the degree of the polynomial p(x)

name: Order p-squared Group Commutativity Theorem
original_full_statement: If G is a finite group of order p^2 for some prime number p, then G is an abelian group.
hypotheses: G is a finite group
The order of G is p^2 for some prime number p
conclusion: G is an abelian group

name: Sylow's Second Theorem
original_full_statement: If G is a finite group and p is a prime dividing the order of G, then any two Sylow p-subgroups of G are conjugate.
hypotheses: G is a finite group
p is a prime number dividing the order of G
P and Q are two Sylow p-subgroups of G
conclusion: P and Q are conjugate subgroups in G

name: Commutator Subgroup Quotient Theorem
original_full_statement: Let G be a group and N be a normal subgroup of G. The quotient group G/N is abelian if and only if the commutator subgroup G' is contained in N.
hypotheses: G is a group
N is a normal subgroup of G
The commutator subgroup of G, denoted G', is a subgroup of N
conclusion: The quotient group G/N is abelian

name: Nonzero Prime Ideal in PID Theorem
original_full_statement: In a principal ideal domain, every non-zero prime ideal is a maximal ideal.
hypotheses: R is a principal ideal domain
I is a non-zero prime ideal of R
conclusion: I is a maximal ideal of R

name: PID Implies Noetherian Theorem
original_full_statement: Every principal ideal domain is a Noetherian ring.
hypotheses: R is a principal ideal domain
conclusion: R is a Noetherian ring

name: Second Isomorphism Theorem for Rings
original_full_statement: Let R be a ring, S be a subring of R, and I be an ideal of R. Then S + I is a subring of R, S intersection I is an ideal of S, and the quotient ring (S + I) / I is isomorphic to S / (S intersection I).
hypotheses: R is a ring
S is a subring of R
I is an ideal of R
conclusion: The quotient ring (S + I) / I is isomorphic to the quotient ring S / (S intersection I)

name: Finite Extension Implies Algebraic Theorem
original_full_statement: If K is a finite extension of a field F, then K is an algebraic extension of F.
hypotheses: K is a field extension of a field F
The degree of the extension [K:F] is finite
conclusion: K is an algebraic extension of F

name: Subfields of a Finite Field Theorem
original_full_statement: Let F be a finite field of order p^n. For every positive divisor m of n, there exists a unique subfield of F of order p^m.
hypotheses: F is a finite field of order p^n for some prime p and positive integer n
m is a positive integer that divides n
conclusion: F contains a unique subfield of order p^m

name: Legendre's Formula
original_full_statement: For any prime p and any positive integer n, the p-adic valuation of n!, which is the exponent of the highest power of p that divides n!, is given by the sum of floor(n / p^k) for k >= 1.
hypotheses: n is a positive integer
p is a prime number
conclusion: The exponent of the highest power of p dividing n! is equal to the sum from k=1 to infinity of floor(n / p^k)

name: Multiplicativity of the Euler Totient Function
original_full_statement: The Euler totient function is multiplicative, meaning that if m and n are relatively prime positive integers, then phi(mn) = phi(m)phi(n).
hypotheses: m and n are positive integers
The greatest common divisor of m and n is 1
conclusion: phi(mn) = phi(m)phi(n), where phi is the Euler totient function

name: Cyclic Quotient by Center Theorem
original_full_statement: If the quotient group G/Z(G) is cyclic, where Z(G) is the center of G, then G is abelian.
hypotheses: G is a group
Z(G) is the center of G
The quotient group G/Z(G) is cyclic
conclusion: G is an abelian group

name: N/C Theorem
original_full_statement: If H is a subgroup of a group G, then the quotient group N_G(H)/C_G(H) is isomorphic to a subgroup of the automorphism group of H.
hypotheses: G is a group
H is a subgroup of G
N_G(H) is the normalizer of H in G
C_G(H) is the centralizer of H in G
conclusion: The quotient group N_G(H)/C_G(H) is isomorphic to a subgroup of Aut(H)

name: Groups of Order pq Theorem
original_full_statement: Let p and q be primes with p < q. If p does not divide q - 1, then any group of order pq is cyclic.
hypotheses: G is a finite group of order pq
p and q are prime numbers
p is strictly less than q
p does not divide q - 1
conclusion: G is a cyclic group

name: Ideal Union Theorem
original_full_statement: Let I and J be ideals of a ring R. If the union I ∪ J is an ideal of R, then either I ⊆ J or J ⊆ I.
hypotheses: R is a ring
I is an ideal of R
J is an ideal of R
The set union I ∪ J is an ideal of R
conclusion: Either I is a subset of J, or J is a subset of I

name: Irreducible implies Prime in UFD
original_full_statement: In a unique factorization domain, every irreducible element is a prime element.
hypotheses: R is a unique factorization domain (UFD)
p is an irreducible element in R
conclusion: p is a prime element in R

name: Gauss's Lemma for Polynomial Contents
original_full_statement: Let R be a unique factorization domain. The content of the product of two non-zero polynomials in R[x] is equal to the product of their contents, up to multiplication by a unit in R.
hypotheses: R is a unique factorization domain (UFD)
f and g are non-zero polynomials in the polynomial ring R[x]
conclusion: The content of the product fg is associated to the product of the content of f and the content of g

name: Ideals of a Field Theorem
original_full_statement: A field F has exactly two ideals: the zero ideal {0} and the field F itself.
hypotheses: F is a field
I is an ideal of F
conclusion: Either I = {0} or I = F

name: Coprime Degrees Composite Extension Theorem
original_full_statement: Let E and F be finite field extensions of a base field K, contained in a common field. If their degrees [E:K] and [F:K] are relatively prime, then the degree of the composite extension [EF:K] is equal to the product [E:K][F:K].
hypotheses: K is a field
E and F are finite field extensions of K
E and F are subfields of a common larger field
The degrees [E:K] and [F:K] are relatively prime integers
conclusion: The degree of the composite field extension [EF:K] is equal to [E:K] multiplied by [F:K]

name: Gauss's Totient Sum Theorem
original_full_statement: For any positive integer n, the sum of Euler's totient function φ(d) over all positive divisors d of n is equal to n.
hypotheses: n is a positive integer
conclusion: The sum of φ(d) for all positive divisors d of n equals n

name: Law of Quadratic Reciprocity
original_full_statement: For any two distinct odd primes p and q, the Legendre symbol (p/q) times (q/p) is equal to (-1)^(((p-1)/2)((q-1)/2)).
hypotheses: p is an odd prime number
q is an odd prime number
p and q are distinct
conclusion: The product of the Legendre symbols (p/q) and (q/p) equals (-1)^(((p-1)/2)((q-1)/2))

name: Product of Subgroups Order Theorem
original_full_statement: If H and K are finite subgroups of a group G, then the number of elements in the product set HK is equal to (|H| * |K|) / |H ∩ K|.
hypotheses: Let G be a group
Let H be a finite subgroup of G
Let K be a finite subgroup of G
conclusion: The cardinality of the set HK = {hk | h ∈ H, k ∈ K} is given by |H||K|/|H ∩ K|

name: Automorphism Group of a Cyclic Group Theorem
original_full_statement: The automorphism group of a cyclic group of finite order n is isomorphic to the multiplicative group of units modulo n, (ℤ/nℤ)^×.
hypotheses: Let G be a cyclic group
Let the order of G be a finite integer n
conclusion: The automorphism group Aut(G) is isomorphic to the multiplicative group of integers modulo n, (ℤ/nℤ)^×

name: Frattini's Argument
original_full_statement: Let G be a finite group, H a normal subgroup of G, and P a Sylow p-subgroup of H. Then G = H N_G(P), where N_G(P) is the normalizer of P in G.
hypotheses: Let G be a finite group
Let H be a normal subgroup of G
Let P be a Sylow p-subgroup of H
conclusion: G = H N_G(P), where N_G(P) is the normalizer of P in G

name: Reduced Quotient Ring Theorem
original_full_statement: Let R be a commutative ring and I a proper ideal of R. The quotient ring R/I is a reduced ring (has no non-zero nilpotent elements) if and only if I is a radical ideal.
hypotheses: Let R be a commutative ring
Let I be a proper ideal of R
conclusion: The quotient ring R/I has no non-zero nilpotent elements if and only if I is equal to its own radical

name: Polynomial Ring over a Field is Euclidean Theorem
original_full_statement: If F is a field, then the polynomial ring F[x] in a single variable over F is a Euclidean domain.
hypotheses: Let F be a field
Let F[x] be the ring of polynomials in a single variable over F
conclusion: F[x] is a Euclidean domain with respect to the polynomial degree function

name: Nilradical Intersection Theorem
original_full_statement: In a commutative ring with identity, the nilradical (the set of all nilpotent elements) is equal to the intersection of all prime ideals of the ring.
hypotheses: Let R be a commutative ring with identity
Let Nil(R) be the nilradical of R, defined as the set of all nilpotent elements in R
conclusion: Nil(R) is identically equal to the intersection of all prime ideals of R

name: Splitting Field Uniqueness Theorem
original_full_statement: Any two splitting fields of a given non-constant polynomial over a field F are isomorphic via an isomorphism that fixes F pointwise.
hypotheses: Let F be a field
Let p(x) be a non-constant polynomial in the polynomial ring F[x]
Let K and L be splitting fields for p(x) over F
conclusion: There exists a field isomorphism ϕ: K → L such that ϕ(a) = a for all a ∈ F

name: Dedekind's Linear Independence of Characters Theorem
original_full_statement: Let G be a group and F a field. Any set of distinct group homomorphisms from G to the multiplicative group F^× is linearly independent over F.
hypotheses: Let G be a group
Let F be a field
Let χ_1, χ_2, ..., χ_n be distinct group homomorphisms from G to the multiplicative group F^×
conclusion: The set of functions {χ_1, χ_2, ..., χ_n} is linearly independent over F

name: Mobius Inversion Formula
original_full_statement: Let f and g be arithmetic functions. If g(n) = ∑_{d|n} f(d) for all positive integers n, then f(n) = ∑_{d|n} μ(d)g(n/d) for all positive integers n, where μ is the Mobius function.
hypotheses: Let f and g be arithmetic functions from the set of positive integers to the complex numbers
Assume that for all positive integers n, g(n) = ∑_{d|n} f(d)
conclusion: For all positive integers n, f(n) = ∑_{d|n} μ(d) g(n/d), where μ is the Mobius function

name: Polynomial Multiple Roots Derivative Theorem

hypotheses: Let F be a field

name: Fixed Field of a Galois Extension Theorem

name: Coprime Powers Theorem

name: Lucas' Theorem
original_full_statement: For any prime p and any non-negative integers m and n, the binomial coefficient C(m, n) is congruent modulo p to the product of the binomial coefficients C(m_i, n_i), where m_i and n_i are the digits of m and n in base p.
